method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar ended Monday higher against every major currency, as US factory surveys came in firmer than expected and kept a December Federal Reserve hike in view. The gains were small: the Fed is expected to hold on Wednesday, October 28, and what Chair Kevin Warsh says about December matters most.

EUR.text: The euro led major currencies on Monday, near $1.12, as French borrowing costs fell after Moody's held France's rating and German firms grew more hopeful. The European Central Bank is expected to hold at 2.5% on Thursday, October 29, and still leans toward more hikes; stress over France's budget is the main reason it might go slower.

GBP.text: The pound eased on Monday as euro-area news improved, even though British shops said sales fell at the slowest pace in about 18 months. Chancellor John Healey is expected to deliver a careful budget on Wednesday, October 28, to keep UK bond investors calm; any borrowing surprise is the pound's biggest risk before a likely Bank of England hike on November 5.

JPY.text: The yen slipped to about 157.5 per dollar on Monday, the weakest of the majors, as shares rose and Gulf talks calmed nerves. The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on Friday, October 30, but may say its 2% inflation goal has been reached, which would point to a December hike and help the yen.

CHF.text: The franc is near a three-month high against the euro after last week's rush to shelter. Monday's talks in Tehran ended with a promise to keep talking, and French bond markets calmed, which takes some of that demand away.

CAD.text: Most economists expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates to 2.50% on Wednesday, October 28, which supports the loonie. But Brent oil's drop to about $110 on Gulf diplomacy cuts into the income Canada earns from oil.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar is near 70 US cents. Inflation figures due Wednesday are expected to stay well above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, and markets give about a 70% chance of a fifth hike this year on November 3.

NZD.text: The kiwi slipped to about 56.9 US cents on Monday as the dollar firmed. Markets see an 85% chance the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raises its rate to 3.00% on Wednesday, October 28, so its hints about further hikes will matter more than the move itself.

XAU.text: Gold closed Monday near $4,013, up slightly, as falling oil eased some inflation worries. A likely US rate hike in December weighs on it, since gold pays no interest, while the unresolved Iran conflict keeps some shelter demand; Wednesday's Federal Reserve decision matters most next.

OIL.text: Brent oil ended Monday near $115, down about 1%, as Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials met Iran's leaders and agreed to keep talking. Nothing concrete was agreed, Iran says ships in the Strait of Hormuz must follow its rules for good, and Yemen's Houthi rebels keep firing at Saudi oil sites, so supply worries have not gone.

items.headline: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk
items.story_title: BoJ: the road to the next hike
items.summary: Japanese bank MUFG expects the Bank of Japan to keep its rate at 1.25% on Friday, October 30, but to say for the first time that underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. That would point toward a hike in December.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan raised its rate to 1.25% in September, and two of its nine board members voted against that hike. The yen is weak, at about 157 per US dollar, partly because Japanese rates are far below US ones.
beats.happened: In a preview of this week's two-day meeting, MUFG said the bank will likely hold but declare in its new forecasts that the 2% inflation goal has been met, and that Governor Kazuo Ueda should sound firm afterwards. A Nikkei report citing a senior official said a second hike in a row is unlikely.
beats.means: A hold that clearly opens the door to a December hike would help the yen. The main risk is the two members who opposed September's move: if they push for easier policy, the firm message gets muddied.
beats.fx: Hold + 'inflation goal reached' → December hike bets rise → support for the yen. Votes for easier policy would cut against that.

impact.why: A firm hold would bring a December hike closer, which supports the yen; a preview, not news.

items.watch: Friday's Bank of Japan statement, its new inflation forecasts and how many members vote against.

items.headline: Financial & Forex Market Recap: Oct. 26, 2026
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: The US dollar ended Monday higher against all seven other major currencies, helped by strong US factory surveys, even as oil fell and shares rose. The dollar index closed near 102.0, up about 0.2%.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time in about three years and is expected to hold at 3.75%–4.00% on Wednesday, October 28. Markets think another hike could come in December.
beats.happened: The dollar rose about 0.4% against the yen to near 157.5 and about 0.2% against the euro and pound, which closed near $1.118 and $1.335. US oil fell about 1.7% to near $103, gold closed near $4,013, and the 10-year US Treasury yield ended near 4.99%. Reports from the Chicago and Dallas Federal Reserve banks showed activity firmer than expected.
beats.means: Solid US data keep a December Fed hike in view, which supports the dollar into Wednesday's decision. The gains were small, so the market is mostly waiting for the Fed.
beats.fx: Firm US data → December hike stays in view → mild support for the dollar across the board.

impact.why: Rose against every major currency on firm US data, though only modestly before the Fed.
Fell most among majors as calmer markets cut demand for shelter.

items.watch: US durable goods orders for September on Tuesday, then the Fed decision on Wednesday.

items.headline: Markets today: U.S. stocks climb and recover last week's losses
items.story_title: Five central banks decide this week
items.summary: US shares rose on Monday afternoon and won back last week's losses, while the 10-year US government bond yield slipped just under 5%. Investors are calmer heading into a week of big company results and central-bank decisions.

beats.was: US shares fell last week on worries about the cost of the AI building boom and the Iran conflict. The 10-year US Treasury yield, a benchmark for borrowing costs, had climbed above 5.30% earlier in October.
beats.happened: By early afternoon in New York the S&P 500 was up 0.8% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 1.1%. The 10-year yield was 4.98%, from 5.00% on Friday, and Brent oil was near $111 after dipping toward $109 in the morning.
beats.means: Investors are more willing to take risk as oil eases on Gulf diplomacy. Lower long-term US yields take a little shine off the dollar, while a calmer mood weighs on shelter currencies like the yen.
beats.fx: Calmer markets and slightly lower US yields → less need for shelter → mixed for the dollar, mild pressure on the yen.

impact.why: Lower long-term yields trim its appeal, but calmer markets give no reason to sell it hard.
Rising shares and calmer markets reduce demand for the yen as a shelter.

items.watch: Wednesday's Fed decision and results from Alphabet and Microsoft the same day.

items.headline: Crude Oil Edges Lower; Chicago Fed Activity Index Rises In September
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: A broad Chicago Fed gauge of the US economy turned slightly positive in September, meaning growth ran just above its normal pace. It is a minor report and the dollar barely moved.

beats.was: The Chicago Fed National Activity Index blends 85 US figures on output, jobs, spending and housing into one number. Zero means the economy is growing at its long-run average pace; it was slightly below zero in August.
beats.happened: The index rose to +0.07 for September from -0.08 in August, published Monday by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
beats.means: The US economy was holding up into the autumn, not speeding up. That fits a Federal Reserve that still sees room to raise rates in December, but it changes little before Wednesday's decision.
beats.fx: Steady US growth → no reason for the Fed to soften → a small, quiet support for the dollar.

impact.why: Growth ran slightly above normal in September; a minor report that moved little.

items.watch: Thursday's first estimate of US growth for July to September, a much bigger report.

items.headline: US October Dallas Fed manufacturing index 13.4 vs 9.8 prior
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: Texas factories said business improved again in October and they feel much better about the next six months. But new orders slowed sharply and the costs they pay kept rising.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas asks Texas manufacturers each month whether business is getting better or worse; any reading above zero means more firms say better. It was 9.8 in September.
beats.happened: The main index rose to 13.4 in October. Firms' outlook for six months ahead jumped to 38.1 from 20.8, but new orders fell to 9.3 from 30.7 and the gauge of prices firms pay rose to 55.3 from 52.2.
beats.means: Factories are still growing, and their own costs are climbing. Several firms blamed fuel prices and high interest rates. Rising costs fit the case for a December Fed hike, but the drop in orders is a warning about demand.
beats.fx: Firm activity and rising costs → keeps a December Fed hike on the table → a small support for the dollar.

impact.why: Business improved and costs kept rising; a regional survey, so the effect is small.

items.watch: Wednesday's Fed decision, and Thursday's first estimate of US growth for July to September.

items.headline: Australian Dollar: Inflation data to bolster yield edge – BBH
items.story_title: RBA: a fifth hike on November 3?
items.summary: US bank Brown Brothers Harriman expects Wednesday's Australian inflation figures to stay well above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts. That would back a fifth rate rise this year on November 3.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its rate four times this year, to 4.60% in September. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser recently said the inflation outlook is much worse than the bank thought in August.
beats.happened: BBH expects yearly inflation for September to rise to 4.2% from 4.0%, and the trimmed mean, a core measure that drops the biggest price swings, to stay at 3.6%. Both are above the bank's year-end forecasts of 3.6% and 3.3%. Markets put the chance of a hike to 4.85% on November 3 at about 70%.
beats.means: Another hike would widen the gap between Australian and other countries' interest rates, which makes the Australian dollar more attractive to hold.
beats.fx: Inflation above forecast → November hike more likely → wider rate gap → support for the Australian dollar.

impact.why: A preview: hot inflation would firm up a November hike, but much of it is already priced.

items.watch: Australia's September and third-quarter inflation figures, out Wednesday, October 28 (late Tuesday in the US).

items.headline: Morning Kickstart: Dollar higher as Fed, earnings and data flood loom
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: The dollar firmed against every major currency before New York opened, gaining most on the yen and the New Zealand dollar. A packed US week starts here: the Fed on Wednesday, then growth and inflation figures on Thursday.

beats.was: The dollar ended last week near a three-week low after falling US bond yields and a slide in big tech shares. Markets still expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December.
beats.happened: On Monday morning the dollar rose to about 157.35 yen and the New Zealand dollar slipped to about 56.8 US cents. The euro and pound eased a little. Oil fell again on Iran diplomacy, and US stock futures pointed higher.
beats.means: A small bounce, not a turn. Buyers are getting into position before the Fed decision on Wednesday, October 28, and Thursday's first estimate of US growth for July to September plus the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
beats.fx: Fed expected to stay firm → US rates stay attractive → mild support for the dollar, mostly against low-yielding currencies like the yen.

impact.why: Up against all major currencies in early trade, ahead of a busy Fed week.
Gave back part of last week's gain; the biggest mover against the dollar.
Slipped about 0.3% before Wednesday's Reserve Bank of New Zealand decision.

items.watch: What Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says about December on Wednesday; a softer tone would undo the bounce.

items.headline: NZD Nears 0.5700 as Markets Price Further RBNZ Hikes
items.story_title: RBNZ: a third hike on October 28?
items.summary: Markets see about an 85% chance that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raises its rate to 3.00% on Wednesday, October 28, and expect more hikes after that. The kiwi sat near 57 US cents.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has been raising rates as high oil prices and a weak currency push up import costs. Its key rate, the official cash rate, is 2.75%.
beats.happened: Interest-rate markets priced an 85% chance of a quarter-point hike to 3.00% on Wednesday and more than a full percentage point of hikes over the next year, to about 3.75%. US bank BBH said high oil prices support more hikes, but a firmer US Federal Reserve limits how far the kiwi can rise against the dollar.
beats.means: A hike is mostly expected, so the kiwi will react more to what the bank says about December than to the move itself.
beats.fx: Hike mostly priced → the bank's hints about more hikes decide the kiwi's move.

impact.why: More hikes are expected, but the October move is already in the price.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's decision and statement on Wednesday, October 28 (Tuesday evening in the US).

items.headline: Ready for a French test?: Five questions for the ECB
items.story_title: Five central banks decide this week
items.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to keep its main rate at 2.5% on Thursday, with economists looking for another hike in December. The jump in French borrowing costs is the new worry it has to weigh.

beats.was: The ECB raised rates in June and September because oil, up about 90% this year, pushed euro-area inflation to 3.8% in September. France's 10-year borrowing cost then rose above 5%, its highest in over two decades, over a budget fight.
beats.happened: A Reuters preview says the bank will likely hold on October 29 and avoid promising its next step. The gap between French and German 10-year yields has widened to 1.67 percentage points from 0.92 at the last meeting. Markets price at least two more hikes by mid-2027.
beats.means: The ECB still leans toward more hikes, but stress in France could make it go slower, since higher rates would add to France's debt costs. President Christine Lagarde has said France must fix its own finances.
beats.fx: Hikes still expected, but France is a reason to go slow → mixed for the euro.

impact.why: More hikes are expected, but French bond stress could slow them; a preview, so mostly priced.

items.watch: Thursday's ECB decision and what Lagarde says about December and about France.

items.headline: Iran says it controls the Strait of Hormuz and its routes will not go back to how they were
items.story_title: Iran war: the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's top military officer said the Strait of Hormuz is closed to any ship that does not follow Iran's rules, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said shipping there will not return to its pre-war form. The same day, talks in Tehran with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan ended with only a promise to keep talking.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, and traffic there is still restricted; Brent oil is up nearly 90% this year.
beats.happened: On Monday, Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran's armed forces, told troops on the coast that Iran has full control of the strait and ships cannot pass unless they follow Iranian rules. Araghchi said both the routes and the way the strait is run will change for good, and that talks on this will continue.
beats.means: Even if the fighting winds down, Iran wants a lasting say over who uses the strait. That makes a quick return to normal oil shipping less likely, which keeps a floor under prices even as diplomacy calms nerves.
beats.fx: Lasting limits on Hormuz traffic → oil stays dear → support for oil, a cost for big importers like Japan and the euro area. Mostly a restatement of Iran's stance, so the push is small.

impact.why: Signals Hormuz shipping won't fully reopen soon, but repeats Iran's known stance.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so dearer oil weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran publishes concrete rules for ships, and whether tanker traffic through Hormuz picks up or falls.

items.headline: Gold consolidates near $4,000 as recovery remains fragile ahead of Fed decision
items.story_title: Gold: oil, rates and the Fed
items.summary: Gold edged back to about $4,016 an ounce on Monday after falling to its lowest since August last week. Bets on a December US rate hike keep the bounce small.

beats.was: Gold lost nearly 4% last week, dipping to about $3,975, as high oil raised fears of more inflation and more US rate hikes. Gold pays no interest, so it suffers when rates rise.
beats.happened: A slightly weaker dollar and lower US bond yields helped gold up about 0.5%. Markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve hike in December at about 79%.
beats.means: The selling has paused, but the main weight is still there. The Fed's decision on Wednesday, October 28, and what Chair Kevin Warsh says about December, will likely set gold's direction.
beats.fx: More US hikes expected → holding gold costs more in lost interest → pressure on gold. Cheaper oil today eases that a little.

impact.why: A small bounce from a two-and-a-half-month low, with December hike bets still weighing.

items.watch: Whether the Fed signals a December hike on Wednesday; a softer tone would help gold.

items.headline: Strong CBI retail sales buck downbeat UK consumer trend
items.story_title: UK growth before the November 5 Bank of England decision
items.summary: British shops said sales fell at the slowest pace in about 18 months in October, a much better reading than expected. The business group behind the survey still calls the outlook fragile.

beats.was: UK shoppers have been pulling back: official September sales were weak and consumer confidence had its sharpest drop since the pandemic, ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first budget on Wednesday, October 28.
beats.happened: The Confederation of British Industry's monthly retail survey jumped to -10 from -55, far better than the roughly -47 expected. Orders to suppliers also improved from a record low.
beats.means: It eases fears that UK spending is collapsing, which helps the case for a Bank of England hike on November 5. But it is one survey of 68 chains, and the group warns that fuel costs and careful households still weigh.
beats.fx: Spending holds up better than feared → less pressure to go easy on rates → small support for the pound. The pound slipped anyway on Monday, so the effect is minor.

impact.why: A big beat on a survey, but sterling eased anyway with the budget two days away.

items.watch: Wednesday's budget: tax rises that hit spending would undo the relief.

items.headline: Oil plunges more than 6% from near wartime highs as diplomacy over Iran seemingly gathers pace
items.story_title: US–Iran: talks or new strikes?
items.summary: Brent oil fell to about $110 a barrel on Monday morning, from about $117 at Friday's close, as several countries stepped up efforts to stop the US–Iran war flaring again. European shares rose.

beats.was: Oil has been high since the US–Iran war began; Brent was near $72 before it and closed Friday near $117, close to its March peak, after Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked Saudi oil sites and tankers.
beats.happened: Qatari mediators visited Tehran on Sunday in step with Washington, and Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish security chiefs arrived on Monday. President Trump told Fox News the choice is between a deal with Iran or finishing the war by force.
beats.means: Markets are betting that talks lower the chance of new US strikes, so part of the war premium in oil is coming out. Supply is still at risk: the Houthis say they hit Saudi airports and energy sites again over the weekend.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil → less money flowing to oil exporters and less inflation worry for importers → a drag on the Canadian dollar, a small help for the yen. Lower oil also eases pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep raising rates.

impact.why: Diplomacy hopes took a large slice of the war premium out of Brent in one morning.
Canada sells oil abroad, so lower prices trim its income.
Japan buys nearly all its oil, so cheaper crude eases its import bill.

items.watch: Whether the Tehran talks produce anything concrete, or Houthi attacks or US strikes resume.

items.headline: Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to further talks
items.story_title: US–Iran: talks or new strikes?
items.summary: Monday's meeting in Tehran between Iran and senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan ended with a promise to keep talking about regional security. No deal or new arrangement was announced.

beats.was: The US and Israel fought Iran earlier this year, and a shaky pause has held since. US officials say new strikes could come soon, and Yemen's Houthi rebels, backed by Iran, keep attacking Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are partners in a new defence pact signed in Mecca.
beats.happened: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei and President Masoud Pezeshkian hosted Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir and Turkey's intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. A joint statement said they would keep consulting on peace and security. Pezeshkian said Iran does not want nuclear weapons and criticised the US for offering talks while threatening strikes.
beats.means: Regional powers are keeping a channel open, which helps hold off new fighting for now. But nothing concrete came out, and the main gap between Washington and Tehran is unchanged.
beats.fx: Talks continue but no deal → war risk eases only a little → a mild weight on oil prices.

impact.why: Talks keep going, slightly lowering the near-term risk to Gulf supply.
Calmer news takes away a little shelter demand.

items.watch: Whether President Trump chooses a deal or new strikes, and whether Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia ease.

items.headline: Euro tests 0.8400 against British Pound as German business climate beats expectations
items.story_title: UK: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: The pound gave back some ground to the euro on Monday, with the euro near 84 pence after a better German business survey, lower oil and calmer French bond markets.

beats.was: On Friday the pound reached its strongest against the euro since May 2025, near 83.6 pence, helped by strong UK business surveys that make a Bank of England rate hike on November 5 look likely.
beats.happened: The euro rose about 0.3% from Friday's low after Germany's Ifo business survey beat forecasts, Brent oil dropped toward $110 and French yields eased.
beats.means: This is mostly the euro bouncing rather than fresh bad news for Britain. The pound's next big test is Chancellor John Healey's budget on Wednesday, October 28.
beats.fx: Better news from Germany and France → money moves back toward the euro → the pound slips against it. An expected Bank of England hike limits how far it can fall.

impact.why: Pulled back from a 17-month high against the euro as the euro area's news improved.
German firms' brighter outlook and calmer French bonds helped the euro.

items.watch: Healey's budget on October 28: how much borrowing and tax it plans, and how UK government bonds react.

items.headline: Germany Ifo business confidence improves in October as expectations surprise higher
items.story_title: Euro area: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: German firms grew more upbeat about the months ahead in October, even though they judged business today a little worse. It is the fifth monthly rise in the Ifo survey of German business mood.

beats.was: The Ifo index asks about 9,000 German companies how business is going now and how they expect it to go over the next six months. Germany is the euro area's biggest economy, and last week's euro-area business surveys showed growth slowing to a four-month low.
beats.happened: The overall reading edged up to 90.2 from 89.9, just above the 90.0 forecast. Hopes for the coming months jumped to their highest since February 2022, while firms' view of current conditions slipped below forecast.
beats.means: German companies expect better times ahead, but today's business is not improving yet, and surveys are not hard data. It softens last week's gloomy euro-area picture without changing it.
beats.fx: Brighter German outlook → slightly less worry about euro-area growth → a small help for the euro. It is unlikely to change the European Central Bank's decision on Thursday, October 29, where a hold is expected. The question to keep asking: is the euro area's slowdown bottoming out?

impact.why: Firms' hopes for the months ahead rose more than expected, though current business weakened.

items.watch: Whether hard data, like factory orders and output, start to follow the brighter outlook.

items.headline: Why is the Euro outperforming at start of ECB policy week?
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: The euro was the best performer among major currencies on Monday morning as the interest rate on French government debt eased further, after Moody's chose not to cut France's credit rating.

beats.was: Worries about France's public debt, a budget fight and street protests pushed France's 10-year borrowing cost to 5.14% last week, its highest in about 20 years, and weighed on the euro.
beats.happened: Moody's kept France at Aa3 with a negative outlook late Friday instead of cutting it. On Monday France's 10-year yield slipped to just under 5%, and the euro rose about 0.25% against the yen.
beats.means: The rating decision gives France some breathing room, and investors are buying French bonds again. The underlying problems, a large deficit and a split parliament, have not gone away.
beats.fx: Lower French borrowing costs → less fear of a euro-area debt scare → support for the euro before the European Central Bank decides on Thursday, October 29.

impact.why: Easing French debt worries remove a weight that hit the euro last week.

items.watch: Whether French yields climb back above 5% as the budget debate in parliament continues.

items.headline: Delegations meeting in Tehran with region on edge over potential for renewed fighting
items.story_title: US–Iran: talks or new strikes?
items.summary: Saudi Arabia's defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief went to Tehran on Monday to try to stop fighting between Iran, Israel and the US from starting again. No result has been reported yet.

beats.was: The US and Israel fought Iran earlier this year, and a shaky pause has held since. Last week US officials said new US strikes could come soon, and Yemen's Houthi rebels, who are backed by Iran, kept attacking Saudi Arabia.
beats.happened: The three delegations met Iran's top security officials to push for a US–Iran deal and to discuss the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, said Iran will not accept the 'complete surrender' US officials ask for.
beats.means: Big regional powers are now working to cool things down, which lowers the odds of a new round of fighting in the short run. The gap between the two sides is still wide.
beats.fx: Less fear of war → less demand for shelter and a smaller war premium in oil → a mild weight on oil and the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Talks lower the near-term risk of new strikes on Gulf supply.
Calmer news takes away a little of the shelter buying that lifted the franc.

items.watch: Any statement from Tehran or Washington after the meetings, and whether Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia stop.

items.headline: UK Finance Minister Healey to Announce Cautious, Market-Minded Budget
items.story_title: UK: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: Britain's finance minister, Chancellor John Healey, is expected to present a careful first budget on Wednesday, aimed at keeping bond investors calm rather than spending big. A higher tax on bank profits is the main expected tax rise.

beats.was: UK government borrowing costs are the highest in the G7, with the 30-year yield near 6% and the 10-year at its highest since 2007. Public debt passed £3 trillion in September, so Healey has little room against his own borrowing rules.
beats.happened: Reuters reports the October 28 budget will offer some help with energy bills and business costs, raise the levy on bank profits, and leave bigger plans from Prime Minister Andy Burnham for a spending review next year. Economists quoted said investors would punish any spending not paid for.
beats.means: A careful budget would ease the risk of another sell-off in UK government bonds, which has weighed on the pound. Any surprise in extra borrowing would be the big danger.
beats.fx: Careful budget → steadier UK bonds → mild support for the pound; a borrowing surprise would hurt it.

impact.why: A careful plan would calm UK bonds, but the budget is still the pound's biggest risk this week.

items.watch: Wednesday's budget: how much the government plans to borrow, and how UK bond yields react.

items.headline: Houthis say they attacked East-West oil pumping stations
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels said they hit pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's main cross-country oil pipeline and Riyadh's airport. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed it, and the Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed two Houthi missile launchers in Sanaa.

beats.was: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have been firing missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil sites, which helped push oil to a six-month high last week. The East-West pipeline carries Saudi crude to the Red Sea, letting it avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: The Houthis claimed new strikes on the pipeline's pumping stations and on Riyadh airport, after warning on Saturday that the airport remains a target. There was no Saudi confirmation of damage. The coalition said it intercepted a missile fired at Riyadh and destroyed the launcher.
beats.means: If the pipeline were damaged, Saudi Arabia would lose its main way around Hormuz. For now these are claims only, and oil fell on Monday anyway, so the market is treating them as contained.
beats.fx: Unconfirmed claims → limited extra supply fear → little lift for oil or the yen today. A confirmed hit would change that fast. The question to keep asking: is Saudi oil actually being disrupted?

impact.why: A hit on the pipeline would matter, but the claims are unconfirmed.
More fighting in the Gulf can send money to the yen for safety.

items.watch: Saudi confirmation or denial of damage to the East-West pipeline.

items.headline: Deal or ‘finish it off’: Donald Trump says ‘decision time’ on Iran near
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he is close to choosing between a deal with Iran and renewed attacks. He said there would be no strike that day, and has hinted strikes could wait until after the November 3 US elections.

beats.was: The US and Iran are in a war that has paused but not ended. Regional mediators are in Tehran trying to head off new US strikes, while Yemen's Houthi rebels, allied with Iran, keep firing at Saudi targets.
beats.happened: In a Fox News interview Trump said it is nearly time to decide: make a deal or finish the campaign by force. The US has sent a third aircraft carrier group to the Gulf, and Bloomberg reports Iran is preparing to hit back across the region if bombed.
beats.means: Diplomacy is moving, but the threat of new strikes is back on a clock. The weeks after the US vote look like the riskiest window, which keeps a war premium in oil even as prices fall.
beats.fx: Risk of renewed strikes → supply fears for Gulf oil → upward pressure on oil and some demand for safe currencies. Oil still fell on Monday, so for now the talks outweigh the threat.

impact.why: Keeps the risk of new fighting alive, though oil fell on the talks.
Mild shelter demand if strikes look closer.
Mild shelter demand if strikes look closer.

items.watch: Any result from the talks in Tehran, or a firm date for strikes; Israel's election on Tuesday, October 27, could also change the picture.

items.headline: US has plans for major Iran strikes if Trump chooses
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Two US officials told CNN that American forces in the Middle East could start large new attacks on Iran within four days of an order from President Donald Trump. No decision has been made; officials see the weeks after the November 3 US elections as the most likely window.

beats.was: The US and Iran fought earlier this year, then Trump halted full combat; since then the US has made only small strikes on radars and missile launchers, and blocks Iran's ports near the Strait of Hormuz. Gulf mediators are now in Tehran trying to head off a new round.
beats.happened: CNN reports enough US forces are already in place for a much bigger campaign, with a target list that includes Iran's energy sites, military bases and nuclear facilities. The US embassy in Riyadh has ordered non-essential staff out, and US intelligence expects Iran and Yemen's Houthi rebels to hit back fast if attacked.
beats.means: The threat behind Trump's 'deal or force' choice is concrete, not just talk. Officials note he has stepped back at the last minute before, so this raises the odds of new fighting without making it certain.
beats.fx: Possible strikes on Iran's energy sites → risk to Gulf oil supply → upward pressure on oil and some demand for safe currencies. Oil still fell on Monday, so markets are giving the talks more weight for now.

impact.why: Energy sites are on the reported target list, but oil fell on the talks.
Mild shelter demand if strikes look closer.
Mild shelter demand if strikes look closer.
Gold edged up to about $4,025 as war risk lingers.

items.watch: Whether the talks in Tehran produce anything before the US elections on November 3, and any further drawdown of US embassy staff in the Gulf.

items.headline: Currency markets subdued ahead of pivotal central bank week
items.story_title: Five central banks decide this week
items.summary: Currencies barely moved on Monday as traders waited for five central-bank decisions this week. The Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan are expected to hold; Canada and New Zealand may raise rates.

beats.was: Oil above $110 has kept inflation high this year, so most central banks are leaning toward raising rates. Last week a slide in US tech shares sent money into US government bonds, pulling yields down and the dollar near a three-week low.
beats.happened: The euro sat near $1.12, the pound near $1.34 and the yen near 157 per dollar, all within a fraction of Friday. Oil eased after Qatari mediators went to Tehran. The Federal Reserve decides on Wednesday, October 28, along with the Bank of Canada and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand; the European Central Bank follows on Thursday and the Bank of Japan on Friday.
beats.means: The decisions themselves are mostly expected, so what each bank says about its next meetings will matter more. US interest rates have been setting the dollar's direction lately, and the gap between US rates and others has been narrowing.
beats.fx: Smaller rate gap between the US and others → less reason to hold dollars → a mild drag on the dollar. Canada and New Zealand hiking would support their currencies only if they signal more to come. The question to keep asking: who sounds readier to raise rates again?

impact.why: Lower US yields weigh, but a December Fed hike is still largely expected.
Markets expect a Bank of Canada hike on Wednesday.
Markets expect a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on Wednesday.

items.watch: What Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says about December at Wednesday's press conference (1:30 PM CT).

items.headline: Oil drops from near six-month highs on hopes Iran war hostilities to ease
items.story_title: US–Iran: talks or new strikes?
items.summary: Oil fell more than 1% on Monday, with Brent near $115, after Qatari mediators went to Tehran with US backing and the weekend passed without a US strike on Iran.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea is still disrupted. Brent rose about 6% last week, to its highest in six months, as Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked Saudi oil sites, and a US envoy warned a strike on Iran could come over the weekend.
beats.happened: No strike came. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Sunday in a push to calm tensions, coordinated with the US, and officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were due to meet Iran's leaders on Monday. Brent fell about $1.50 to around $115.
beats.means: Some of the fear that drove last week's jump is fading, but the supply risks are still there. Analysts quoted say the relief may not last, and the head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, expects energy markets to stay disrupted through 2027.
beats.fx: Talks instead of strikes → less fear of a supply cut → oil eases → less need for shelter, so a little less support for the yen, and a small drag on the oil-linked Canadian dollar. The question to keep asking: is the Gulf heading toward talks or more fighting?

impact.why: Mediation in Tehran and a quiet weekend took some of the war fear out of the price.
Less war fear means less buying of the yen for safety.
Cheaper oil trims Canada's export income.

items.watch: Any outcome from Monday's Tehran meetings, or a new Houthi strike on Saudi oil.

items.headline: Japanese Yen holds near one-month top vs weak USD as traders await Fed, BoJ meetings
items.story_title: BoJ: the road to the next hike
items.summary: The yen held near its strongest in a month, just under 157 per dollar, ahead of the Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of Japan on Friday.

beats.was: The yen had been weak for months because Japan's interest rates are far below US rates. Last week it gained as falling shares and war worries sent money to shelter, and the dollar touched about 156, its lowest against the yen since mid-September.
beats.happened: The dollar's small bounce stalled below 157 yen. Lower US bond yields are holding the dollar back, while Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda has recently said underlying inflation is nearing the bank's 2% goal, a sign a rate hike is getting closer.
beats.means: The gap between US and Japanese interest rates may be starting to narrow from both sides: US yields have eased and Japan is edging toward a hike. Friday's Bank of Japan meeting is expected to keep rates at 1.25%, so its hints about the next move matter most.
beats.fx: Narrower US–Japan rate gap → less reward for borrowing in yen to buy dollars → support for the yen. The question to keep asking: how close is the Bank of Japan to its next hike?

impact.why: Lower US yields and hints of a Bank of Japan hike support the yen.
Falling US bond yields limit the dollar's bounce.

items.watch: Bank of Japan decision and Governor Ueda's comments on Friday, October 30.

items.headline: RBA's Hunter says inflation job not done after four hikes, November rise in view
items.story_title: RBA: a fifth hike on November 3?
items.summary: Sarah Hunter, an Assistant Governor at the Reserve Bank of Australia, said on TV that the bank has not yet done enough to bring inflation down. Markets already expect a fifth rate hike this year on November 3.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its cash rate four times this year, most recently in late September, to 4.6%, a 15-year high. Higher oil prices from the US–Iran war are pushing costs up.
beats.happened: In a 60 Minutes interview on Sunday, Hunter said the job is 'not quite yet' done and that higher oil costs are spreading through supply chains. She did not say what the board will decide.
beats.means: A senior official is backing up what markets already expect: another hike next week. Third-quarter inflation figures on Wednesday, October 28 are the last big test before the decision.
beats.fx: Hawkish tone → Australian rates stay high or go higher → mild support for the Australian dollar, which is already near a one-month high above 70 US cents.

impact.why: An official backed the November hike that markets already price.

items.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figures on October 28; a soft reading would cast doubt on the hike.

items.headline: Hundreds of thousands protest in France amid heightened police security
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: About 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, by the government's count, over school conditions and living costs. Marches were mostly peaceful, with about 1,000 arrests, fewer than the week before.

beats.was: Protests over run-down schools, teacher shortages and the cost of living turned into looting and violence a week earlier, adding to worries about France's budget and debt.
beats.happened: The Interior Ministry counted 410,000 marchers, 110,000 of them in Paris; unions said about twice that. More than 70,000 police were deployed and several marches were banned or moved. Police made nearly 1,000 arrests, against more than 2,000 after the October 17 protests.
beats.means: Calmer than the week before, but students say they will keep marching until they see action. Ongoing unrest makes it harder for the government to pass spending cuts.
beats.fx: Lasting unrest → harder to cut the deficit → investors want more to hold French debt → a mild drag on the euro. The question to keep asking: is the unrest fading or spreading?

impact.why: Unrest makes a deficit-cutting budget harder, though this weekend was calmer.

items.watch: Whether students and unions call more marches, and how parliament votes on the budget.
